questions.learningObjective: read the common difference off an arithmetic sequence
questions.stem: The sequence 4, 9, 14, 19, ... is generated by adding the same amount each time. What is that amount?

names a term of the sequence as the size of the jump
assumes a step of 1 because the terms rise one place at a time

The tempting error is 5 + 20(4) = 85, which has taken twenty jumps instead of nineteen.

starts the pattern at zero and takes ten steps of 5

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: state the convergence condition for a geometric series
questions.stem: For which values of the common ratio r does the geometric series 1 + r + r^2 + r^3 + ... converge to a finite sum?

options.text: |r| < 1, since only then do the terms shrink fast enough to be summable
r > 0, since a positive ratio always drives the terms down to zero
options.misconception: restricts convergence to positive ratios and forgets negative ones

options.text: |r| = 1, since at that size the terms stop growing
options.misconception: thinks a constant term size is enough to make a sum finite

options.text: |r| > 1, since a large ratio makes the later terms negligible
options.misconception: reverses the size test and treats growth as decay

questions.explanation: The geometric series sums to a_1/(1 − r) only when |r| < 1, and that is exactly the range in which r^n tends to zero. The reason is that a finite sum can absorb infinitely many terms only if the tail keeps shrinking, so the terms themselves must approach zero. For |r| = 1 the terms never shrink, and for |r| > 1 they grow, so no finite sum can exist in either case.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the terms r^n as n grows without bound.

the sum really is -1/2, because the formula a_1/(1 − r) has no restrictions

computes the last term as 5 + 12(4) instead of 5 + 11(4)

questions.stem: Why is 1/(1·2) + 1/(2·3) + 1/(3·4) + ... described as a telescoping sum?

the denominators grow by one at each step, which is what telescoping means

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: prove the sum of the first n odd numbers equals n squared
questions.stem: Prove that the sum of the first n odd numbers, 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n − 1), equals the square of n.

answer.exemplar: Add the sum to the same sum written in reverse order. Column by column the two rows give 1 + (2n − 1), 3 + (2n − 3), and so on, and every one of these pairs adds to 2n. There are n such columns, so the total of the two rows together is 2n times n, which is twice the original sum, and dividing by two gives n². Induction confirms the identity, because n² + (2n + 1) = n² + 2n + 1 = (n + 1)², so the formula holds at n + 1 whenever it holds at n, and the base case n = 1 is 1 = 1². Having two routes agree is what turns the pairing into a proof rather than a lucky pattern.

questions.explanation: A model answer must justify both the pairing that doubles the sum and the division by two that recovers it, since either step alone leaves the argument incomplete.
questions.hint: Write the sum twice, once in reverse order, and examine what each column adds to.

options.text: that the base case n = 1 already covers every later index
options.misconception: treats one verified case as though it verified them all

The step adds the next term, n + 1, giving n(n + 1)/2 + (n + 1), and this must simplify to the formula at index n + 1, which is (n + 1)(n + 2)/2. Factoring the left side as (n + 1)(n/2 + 1) = (n + 1)(n + 2)/2 shows the two agree. The third option is the subtlest trap, because it leaves the target formula unchanged and so proves nothing about n + 1.
questions.hint: Add the term n + 1 to the hypothesis and check that the result is the formula at n + 1.

questions.learningObjective: count assignments of distinct roles to distinct people

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: explain when counting multiplies and when it adds
questions.stem: A cafeteria offers 5 mains, 4 sides and 3 desserts. A three-course meal takes one of each, while a two-course meal is either a main with a side or a main with a dessert. Explain why the three-course count multiplies and the two-course count adds.

answer.exemplar: A three-course meal is assembled in three successive stages, and every stage is chosen independently of the others, so the multiplication rule applies: 5 · 4 · 3 = 60. Choosing the main first does not restrict the side or the dessert, and each of the 5 mains can be paired with each of the 4 sides and each of the 3 desserts. A two-course meal is not one meal with stages; it is a choice between two kinds of meal, and the two kinds are disjoint because no single meal is both a main with a side and a main with a dessert. The sum rule therefore gives 5 · 4 + 5 · 3 = 35, where each product handles one kind and the addition combines the kinds. Multiplying the two kinds together, at 5 · 4 · 5 · 3, would falsely insist that a two-course meal also contain a dessert.

questions.explanation: A model answer must say what makes the three stages independent and what makes the two kinds mutually exclusive, since those are the two conditions the two rules require.
questions.hint: Ask whether the stages are independent, and whether the two kinds can overlap.

Every distinct arrangement is therefore counted 2! · 2! = 4 times, so the answer is 5040/4 = 1260. The other repeated letters do not matter because the two Bs are distinguishable, and dividing by more than 4 would undercount arrangements that genuinely differ.

treats the girls as one indivisible unit with no internal order
arranges the four units but forgets the order inside the block

The reason a division is not needed is that fixing the reference person removes the rotational freedom at the start. A mirror image is a different seating, because it reverses the clockwise order, so nothing is divided by 2.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: justify the n minus one factorial count for circular arrangements
questions.stem: Explain why the number of ways to seat 6 people around a round table, where two seatings that differ only by a rotation count as the same, is 5! and not 6!.

answer.exemplar: Count arrangements around a table with numbered seats and the table is fixed, and there are 6! = 720 of them. But rotating the whole seating carries each genuine circular arrangement through all six choices of who occupies seat 1, so every circular arrangement has been counted exactly six times in that total. Dividing by those six repetitions gives 720/6 = 120, which is 5!. Nothing further is divided out, because reflecting the table reverses the clockwise order of the guests and produces a genuinely different arrangement; identifying reflections as well would incorrectly halve the count to 60. The reason the fix works is that choosing a reference person is a genuine restriction of the equivalence, not a loss of arrangements, since each circular seating has exactly one rotation placing that person in the reference seat.

questions.explanation: A model answer must justify dividing by 6 and must also say why no division by 2 is made, since omitting the second point leaves a common error unaddressed.
questions.hint: Count the arrangements with numbered seats, then ask how many times each circular one is repeated.

reads the count of a different colour from the list
assumes the colours are equally likely because three are listed

options.text: compute the probability that no roll shows a 6 and subtract it from 1
add the probabilities of getting exactly one, two, three, four and five sixes
options.misconception: sums five separate cases when one would do

options.text: list all 6^5 ordered outcomes and count those containing at least one 6
options.misconception: enumerates the whole sample space by hand

options.text: raise the probability of a single 6 to the fifth power and use that as the answer
options.misconception: confuses the all-sixes case with the at-least-one case

questions.explanation: The event at least one 6 is the complement of no roll showing a 6, and the complement of no 6 is easy because the five rolls are independent: its probability is (5/6)^5, so the answer is 1 − (5/6)^5. The direct route would need the probabilities of exactly one, two, three, four and five sixes, each computed from a binomial count. The last option is a real trap, because (1/6)^5 is the probability that every roll shows a 6, which is the rarest case of all rather than the one asked for.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: explain how expected value defines a fair game
questions.stem: A game pays 3 dollars with probability 1/4 and 1 dollar with probability 3/4. Explain what it means for the game to be fair, and how the expected value decides the question.

answer.exemplar: The expected value of the payout is the probability-weighted average, (1/4)(3) + (3/4)(1) = 3/4 + 3/4 = 3/2 dollars. That number is not a prediction of any single play but the long-run average, which is what converges as the number of plays grows. The game is called fair when this expected payout equals the entry fee, because then a player who plays many times neither gains nor loses on average, whatever the individual outcomes turn out to be. So an entry fee of 3/2 dollars makes this game fair, a lower fee favours the player and a higher fee favours the house. Crucially, no change of strategy alters this, because the expectation is fixed before any play occurs and a player cannot pick which outcome appears.

questions.explanation: A model answer must compute the weighted average and then compare it with the entry price, since fairness is defined by the equality of those two amounts.
questions.hint: Take the probability-weighted average of the payouts, then ask what entry price equals it.

questions.explanation: The expected value is the weighted average of the two payouts: (1/4)(6) + (3/4)(2) = 6/4 + 6/4 = 3. The two terms happen to be equal here, which is a reminder that the expectation need not lie between the values in proportion to their frequency. Adding the payouts unweighted would give 8, and averaging them without the weights would give 4; both ignore the probabilities that make the expectation meaningful.
questions.hint: Multiply each payout by its probability, then add the products.

questions.explanation: The expected payout is (1/2)(8) + (1/2)(0) = 4, and the game is fair exactly when the entry fee equals that expected payout, so the fee is 4. With this fee the average player neither gains nor loses over many plays, although most single plays lose the 4 dollars. A fee of 8 would be fair only if the 8 dollars were certain, and a fee of 0 would hand the player a free expected gain of 4 dollars per play.
questions.hint: Set the entry fee equal to the probability-weighted average of the payouts.

questions.stem: A student evaluates the sum from k = 1 to 4 of (2k + 1) as 2(1 + 2 + 3 + 4) + 1, which is 21. What is the correct value of the sum?

options.misconception: adds the constant 1 to the sum of the doubled indices once
multiplies each index by 2 and forgets the constant entirely
adds the constant 1 to the sum of the doubled indices twice

questions.explanation: The summand 2k + 1 has a constant that belongs to every term, so the sum is 2(1 + 2 + 3 + 4) + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 20 + 4 = 24, which matches the direct sum 3 + 5 + 7 + 9. The student's 21 keeps only one of the four copies of the constant, and distributing a constant out of a sum is the error being tested: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 is 4, not 1.
questions.hint: Write the four terms out; the constant is repeated once per term.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: compute the expected value of a sum of random rolls
questions.stem: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled and the two numbers shown are added. What is the expected value of the sum?
questions.explanation: Each die is uniform on 1 through 6, so each has expected value (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5, and the expectation of a sum is the sum of the expectations, giving 3.5 + 3.5 = 7. Enumerating all 36 ordered outcomes confirms it, since the 36 sums add to 252 and 252/36 = 7. Independence is not required for the sum rule, though it does hold here.
questions.hint: Find each die's expected value and add the two.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: infer the common difference from two given terms
questions.stem: An arithmetic sequence has a_1 = 5 and a_5 = 5. What does that imply about the sequence?

options.text: the common difference is 0, so every term equals 5
the common ratio is 5, so the terms run 5, 25, 125 and grow
options.misconception: reads a repeated term as evidence of a geometric pattern

options.text: the common difference is 5, so the sequence grows by 5 at every step
options.misconception: confuses the value of the first term with the size of the jump

options.text: nothing follows, because two equal terms cannot determine a sequence
options.misconception: denies the fact that an arithmetic sequence is fixed by two of its terms

questions.explanation: Two terms of an arithmetic sequence determine it, and the common difference is the change between them divided by the number of gaps separating them, here (5 − 5)/4 = 0. A difference of zero means every step leaves the value unchanged, so the sequence is the constant 5. The last option is the tempting one, but it forgets that the sequence is assumed arithmetic, which is exactly the condition that makes the third quantity computable.
questions.hint: Divide the change between two terms by the number of gaps between them.
